lines: Watch what one ordinary event does to two schemas built around the same email address.
One of them simply refuses the change. The other barely notices.
Suppose that email address is the key, referenced everywhere a customer's orders live.
She changes it. What happens to every row that pointed at the old value?
answer: Either the database blocks the update outright, or every one of those references has to be rewritten at once.
Nothing updates itself quietly in the background.

lines: Here is that refusal, happening for real, not described.
An order still points at the email about to change, so the database stops the update cold.
Now swap in a separate, meaningless id for the same job.
The email changes in one row, and every order still finds its way back, because nothing it relies on moved.
That is the whole difference between these two kinds of key.
One borrows meaning from the business and inherits its instability. The other has no meaning to lose.
Now picture several writers, in different places, generating rows with nobody coordinating between them.
Can a plain increasing counter still do the job?
answer: Not safely. A counter like that lives in one place, and every writer needs to ask it for the next number.
That round trip is exactly the coordination a spread-out pipeline is trying to avoid.

lines: The documentation for that counter admits as much, in its own words.
A value it hands out is never undone, so it can't promise no gaps, and letting it hand out several at once breaks the strict order across writers entirely.
So three ways of generating a key were timed against each other, inserting into a table that already had its index built.
The counter came out fastest every time. The time-ordered random id came next. The fully random one was slowest.
Then the shape of each index itself was inspected directly, after all that inserting.
The counter and the time-ordered id both kept their index tight and full. The fully random one left it visibly emptier, spread across more pages for the same number of rows.
Here is why the time-ordered one keeps that tightness.
Its leading bits are a timestamp, so two ids made moments apart share that whole beginning, and land near each other in the index almost by construction.
One more distinction, worth having ready before it matters later in this chapter.
When a row gets versioned over time, something about it has to stay the same across every version, even while its own identifier changes with each one.
One pattern hashes a business attribute instead of generating a fresh id for it.
Is a collision there something to actually worry about, or just a line to mention and move past?
answer: It depends entirely on how wide that hash is.
A wide one is safe by an enormous margin. A narrow one, trimmed down to save space, is not.

lines: Here is that dependence, worked out properly instead of waved at.

A narrow hash reaches even odds of a collision after surprisingly few values. A mid-sized one still carries a real risk once a pipeline grows large. A genuinely wide one does not, by an enormous margin.
One key that borrows meaning breaks when that meaning changes. One that doesn't, absorbs it.
A single counter is fastest but needs one coordinator. The time-ordered id gets most of that speed without one. The fully random id gives up tightness entirely for no coordination at all.
And a hash's safety is a number you can check against your own scale, not a feeling.
One last question before moving on.
Several writers, nobody coordinating, and the key still has to land close to where it was inserted in the index. Which of today's options actually does both?
answer: Nothing coordinates it, and its own leading bits are exactly what keeps it landing close together.
